questions.question_text: What does the expression 7 / 2 + 7 % 2 evaluate to in Java?
questions.explanation: Integer division: 7 / 2 = 3 (truncated, not rounded). Modulus: 7 % 2 = 1. Sum = 4. With two int operands, Java NEVER produces a decimal — expecting 3.5 + 1 = 4.5 is the trap.

questions.question_text: Given String s = "computer";, what does s.substring(3, 6) return?
questions.explanation: substring(3, 6) starts at index 3 (inclusive) and stops before index 6 (exclusive): indices 3,4,5 → 'p','u','t'. Off-by-one errors here come from forgetting the end index is exclusive or starting the count at 1.

questions.question_text: Why does ("hello" == new String("hello")) evaluate to false in Java?
questions.option_b: == compares object references, and these are two different objects
questions.explanation: == on objects checks whether both references point to the SAME object — new String() forces a separate object, so == is false even though the contents match. Use .equals() for content comparison; this distinction appears on nearly every exam.

questions.question_text:
How many times does the body of this loop execute?
for (int i = 1; i <= 10; i += 3)
questions.explanation: i takes values 1, 4, 7, 10 — four iterations; at i = 13 the condition fails. Trace the actual sequence instead of estimating 10/3: the ≤ (not <) lets i = 10 run.
x goes 0 → 2 → 4 → 6; the check happens BEFORE each iteration, so x = 4 < 5 lets one more += 2 run, exiting with 6. The loop can overshoot the bound — the condition limits entry, not the final value.
Valid indices are 0..2 — arr[3] is past the end and throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException at runtime. 'Length 3' means LAST INDEX 2; conflating length with last index is the classic array error.

questions.question_text: list contains ["a", "b", "c", "d"]. After list.remove(1), what does list.get(2) return?
questions.explanation: remove(1) deletes "b" and shifts everything left: ["a", "c", "d"]. Index 2 is now "d". Forgetting the shift — especially when removing inside a loop — is the most common ArrayList bug on the exam.

questions.question_text: For int[][] m = new int[3][4], which expression gives the number of columns?
questions.explanation: A 2D array is an array of rows: m.length = 3 rows, m[0].length = 4 columns. Row-major order matters for nested loop traversal — the outer index selects the row. Option D confuses arrays with ArrayLists.

Java is pass-by-value — but for objects, the VALUE is a reference. a[0] = 99 mutates the shared array; b = 99 only rebinds the local copy of the primitive. Mutating through a reference sticks; reassigning a parameter never does.

questions.option_c: Compile error — Animal has no Dog behavior
questions.explanation: Polymorphism: the declared type (Animal) decides what you MAY call; the runtime object (Dog) decides which override RUNS. Dynamic dispatch always picks the actual object's method — this rule is tested every single year.

questions.question_text: With the classes above, which line causes a compile-time error?
questions.explanation: A superclass object is NOT a Dog — assigning Animal to a Dog reference fails to compile without a cast (and would fail at runtime even with one, since the object isn't actually a Dog). Subtype → supertype widening is automatic; the reverse never is.

questions.question_text:
int f(int n) { if (n <= 1) return 1; return n * f(n - 1); }
What does f(4) return?
questions.explanation: This is factorial: 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24. Trace the unwinding: f(4) = 4·f(3) = 4·3·f(2) = 4·3·2·f(1) = 24. Option B (10) comes from adding instead of multiplying — read the operator.

questions.question_text:
void mystery(int n) { if (n > 0) { mystery(n - 1); System.out.print(n + " "); } }
What does mystery(3) print?
questions.explanation: The print comes AFTER the recursive call, so output happens while the stack unwinds: deepest call (n=1) prints first → 1 2 3. Moving the print before the call would give 3 2 1. Statement position relative to the recursive call controls the order.

questions.question_text: Binary search on a sorted array of 1,024 elements requires at most about how many comparisons?
questions.explanation: Each comparison halves the search space: 2¹⁰ = 1,024, so ~10 steps. That logarithmic behavior is the entire point of binary search — but it REQUIRES sorted data; on unsorted data it's simply wrong, not slow.

questions.question_text: Which statement correctly contrasts selection sort and insertion sort on an already-sorted array?
questions.option_a: Both run in their worst case
questions.option_b: Insertion sort runs in O(n); selection sort still makes O(n²) comparisons
questions.option_c: Selection sort runs in O(n); insertion sort is O(n²)
questions.explanation: Insertion sort exits each pass after one comparison on sorted data (best case O(n)). Selection sort must scan the whole unsorted region for every position regardless — its comparison count never improves. 'Already sorted' is insertion sort's best case, selection sort's same case.

questions.question_text: By De Morgan's laws, !(a && b) is equivalent to:
questions.explanation: Negation distributes by flipping the operator: !(a && b) = !a || !b. Option A keeps && — the most common De Morgan's slip. Verify with a = true, b = false: !(t && f) = true; !t && !f = false ✗; !t || !f = true ✓.

questions.option_b: && short-circuits: the right side never evaluates when the left is false
questions.explanation: Short-circuit evaluation: data != null is false, so data.length never runs. Reversing the operands (data.length > 0 && data != null) WOULD throw — operand order is a safety feature, not style.

questions.question_text: Which keyword makes a variable belong to the class rather than to each instance?
questions.explanation: static = one copy shared by all instances (e.g., a counter of objects created). final means unchangeable; private controls access — orthogonal concepts that the exam likes to mix in one declaration: private static final.
Inner loop runs n, n−1, ..., 1 times → n(n+1)/2 total ≈ n²/2 = O(n²). Starting j at i halves the work but doesn't change the growth class — constants vanish in big-O.

questions.question_text: After int x = 5; x *= 2 + 3;, what is x?
questions.explanation: Compound assignment applies to the WHOLE right side: x = x * (2 + 3) = 25. Reading it as (x * 2) + 3 = 13 is the trap — the right-hand expression evaluates first.
